prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, and so explaining exporter selection, reallocation across firms and a new channel for the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) moved trade theory from representative industries to heterogeneous firms. It explains who exports, why trade liberalisation reallocates resources toward more productive firms, and why gains from trade have a selection component. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple analysis of exporting versus foreign direct investment gives the framework a second, distinct achievement and ties it to firm-level facts. More than twenty years of firm-level evidence from many countries has tested and refined the framework, and it is now standard in trade, macro and industrial organisation. A two-person credit line is clean, and a shortlist candidate with clean attribution is rare. I now put this ahead of my opening first choice, B006, mainly for attribution reasons. The foundational law-and-finance papers have four authors, so a three-person cap cannot honour Vishny, and the legal-origins causal claims are less secure. Hassler raised these points and I accept them as substantive. They are a reason to rank B006 below a cleanly attributable, well-confirmed candidate, whatever its support count.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit and overlap. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely related heterogeneous-firm trade models and the empirical exporter facts, and none of them is on this ballot, so a Melitz-Helpman prize leaves out contributors to the same body of ideas. Krugman's 2008 prize covered adjacent new trade theory, and the welfare gains from selection may be smaller than first claimed once functional-form assumptions (Pareto productivity) and the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare sufficient-statistics results are taken into account. The prize might then be read as honouring a model more than a robust quantitative discovery.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first. She treats Melitz (2003) as the core, with Helpman as the strong second credit through Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. She leaves Redding off as later and more separable, and she flags the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Melitz-Chaney antecedents that are not credited on this list.
responses.response: I agree that the pair is the cleanest cut and that Redding's quantitative spatial and trade work is a separable later contribution. The antecedent problem is real, though, and I would not wave it away. The Bernard et al. Ricardian heterogeneous-firm model is a parallel route, but it is a different structure, and the Committee can only credit names on the ballot. The citation should therefore describe the mechanism (selection, reallocation and the new gains channel) and should not claim to cover everything in the literature. The Melitz-Chaney extension builds on Melitz rather than competing with it, so I do not see it as an obstacle.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B010 second and sees Melitz and Helpman as foundational. He also warns that quantitative work suggests the welfare gains from selection may be smaller than first claimed, and that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum could be viewed as co-originators.
responses.response: I take the size-of-gains point seriously, and it is my main substantive worry. I would still distinguish the size of the gains from the contribution itself. The new facts (exporter premia, within-industry reallocation) and the selection mechanism hold up even where the quantitative welfare effect is modest, and the reassessment of gains from trade is itself a product of the framework. On co-origination, I would rest the case on the Melitz 2003 model and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension, which are documented and ballot-listed, and treat Bernard et al. as a close parallel the Committee should acknowledge in the background rather than a reason to reject the pairing.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 fifth and observes that the legal-origins programme is well cited but contested on identification and robustness. He also notes that a three-person cap forces the exclusion of Vishny, a co-author on the foundational work.
responses.response: This is a fair criticism of my own opening first choice, and it moves me. The exclusion of Vishny from a four-author core is a genuine attribution compromise, and the original anti-director coding and legal-origin causal claims have been criticised. I still think law and finance opened an important empirical programme in comparative corporate finance, so I keep it in view, but I no longer think it is the strongest case once these defects are weighed. I would not describe this as deference to colleagues. The problems you identify bear on merit and credit.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B010 third with a two-person award. He calls Melitz the core and Helpman the extension, treats Redding as the least necessary name, and notes the overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize and with Helpman's role in B041.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person structure. On Krugman, the earlier prize explained trade between similar countries through increasing returns and product variety, whereas this work concerns heterogeneity across firms within industries and the resulting selection and reallocation. I regard it as a distinct contribution and not an increment. Helpman's appearance in other candidacies does not weaken his claim here, because his credit on this ballot rests on the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work, which is specific and well identified.

uncertainties: How the Committee should treat the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum parallel contribution, since those names are not on the ballot.
Whether quantitative critiques of the selection-based gains from trade undercut how the achievement is characterised.
Whether Redding should be added as a third name for quantitative and spatial extensions, which I currently regard as a separable later contribution.
Whether the Committee prefers to recognise trade through a different candidate, such as B003, because of competing claims within the field.
My view of B006 and B016 rests on my own recollection of the literature, not independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Helpman and Melitz. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to the B010 names, and I see none for the B016 or B042 names either. I work in corporate finance, which is close to my opening first choice B006, and I treat that proximity as a possible bias on that candidate, not as a basis for merit.
